mcqs.question: Why can't an API gateway solve the problems a service mesh addresses?
options: Because gateways are always slower than sidecar proxies
Because gateways can only route to a single backend service
Because gateways don't support HTTPS
Because the gateway only sees traffic entering from outside the system, with no visibility into or control over service-to-service (east-west) calls happening internally
mcqs.explanation: A gateway's scope is the system's edge — north-south traffic from external clients. It has no view into calls happening entirely between internal services, which is exactly the east-west traffic problem a mesh is built to handle. Speed, HTTPS support, and routing to multiple backends aren't the actual limitation.

mcqs.question: In a service mesh, what's the key functional difference between the data plane and the control plane?
options: The data plane (sidecar proxies) actually moves and secures every request; the control plane computes configuration and policy and pushes it to the proxies, without touching traffic itself
The data plane stores application data; the control plane stores user credentials
They are two names for the exact same component
The control plane only runs during a deployment, then shuts down
mcqs.explanation: The data plane is the set of proxies handling live traffic on every hop; the control plane is the separate brain that computes routing rules, certificates, and policy and distributes them to proxies, never touching request traffic directly. They are distinct, continuously-running components with different jobs, not aliases or a one-time deploy-time process.

mcqs.question: Why does a service mesh's approach to mTLS and retries generalize well across a polyglot organization (services in Python, Go, Java, etc.)?
options: Because the mesh converts all services to run in a single language
Because the logic lives in the language-agnostic sidecar proxy, so every service gets the same behavior regardless of what language it's written in
Because polyglot organizations don't actually need mTLS
Because the mesh only works with statically-typed languages
mcqs.explanation: Because the sidecar sits outside the application process and intercepts traffic at the network level, it doesn't care what language the service is written in — every service gets identical mTLS and retry behavior for free. The mesh doesn't require language conversion, isn't restricted to any type system, and doesn't reduce the actual need for mTLS.

mcqs.question: What's the real trade-off between handling cross-cutting concerns (retries, mTLS) via a shared library versus via a service mesh?
options: Shared libraries only work with a service mesh already installed
There is no trade-off — a mesh is strictly better in every dimension
A shared library avoids an extra network hop but must be reimplemented per language and redeployed everywhere for a fix; a mesh centralizes the fix but adds a per-call proxy hop
A mesh eliminates all network latency compared to a shared library
mcqs.explanation: A shared library keeps logic in-process (no extra hop) but multiplies maintenance across every language and requires every service to redeploy for a fix; a mesh centralizes the fix in the control plane at the cost of an added proxy hop per call. It's a genuine trade-off, not a strict win either way, and the two approaches aren't dependent on each other.

mcqs.question: Why does sidecar resource overhead matter more at a few thousand Pods than at a few dozen services?
options: It doesn't — sidecar overhead is fixed and identical regardless of Pod count
The overhead is per-instance, so it multiplies with every Pod, turning into a real capacity-planning line item at scale even though it's negligible at small scale
Sidecars only consume resources when actively debugged
Larger clusters automatically disable sidecar resource limits
mcqs.explanation: Each Pod runs its own sidecar, so the CPU/memory cost scales with Pod count, not service count — negligible at small scale, but a real budget item once Pod counts reach the thousands. It isn't a fixed one-time cost, sidecars consume resources continuously, and clusters don't auto-disable their limits at scale.

mcqs.question: A service reports intermittent connection errors, but application logs and traces show nothing unusual. What should be checked next in a meshed environment?
options: Nothing further — if the app shows no issue, the mesh cannot be the cause
The sidecar's own diagnostics (admin endpoint, metrics, logs), since the error could originate in proxy-level configuration invisible to app-level telemetry
Rewrite the application in a different language
Disable the mesh entirely to rule it out
mcqs.explanation: The sidecar operates below the application's own visibility — a misconfigured timeout, tripped circuit breaker, or mTLS failure at the proxy layer won't necessarily show up in app-level logs or traces. Its own admin/diagnostic endpoints are the right next step, not assuming the app's clean logs rule out the mesh, and not a drastic step like disabling the mesh or rewriting the service.
